summary: We have developed a public-facing web tool to display images of the stars from the SPHEREx mission. It uses the SPHEREx database to display a map of the stars, making it user-friendly. By being accessible, it allows people (inexperienced and experienced) to contribute by observing movement and signaling it. People enter the right ascension and declination and are shown the respective patch of the stars; if they notice any changes, they can share information with the community. This tool directly meets the core challenge of transforming the rapidly accumulating SPHEREx all-sky survey (more than a billion objects imaged in 102 near-infrared bands every six months) into an accessible resource for discovery for the most effective observation tool, the human eye, thus all that data that was previously too much was divided and conquered. Our project has been tested on the provided examples. Our tool is easily updatable, makes creative use of the data by providing spectra, has variable FOV for tracking small movements, integrates data from other telescopes (Gaia Mission, WISE Mission), displays metadata, and improves upon tools for handling astronomical data.
details:
Impuls: Multi-Mission 3D Infrared Stellarium & Astrometric Motion Explorer

1. What does it do or how does it work?

Most people think space data looks like polished NASA wallpapers, but in reality, real astrophysics happens in raw, noisy FITS image cubes and multi-wavelength catalogs that are notoriously clunky to work with. I built Impuls to bridge that gap—turning raw multi-mission data into a real-time, interactive 3D observatory in the browser.

Here is the technical pipeline under the hood:

  • Multi-Mission Backend Pipeline: My Python backend (Flask, Astropy, Astroquery, NumPy) interfaces with NASA IRSA and AWS S3 open buckets. It ingests 102 discrete spectral channels across 6 Linear Variable Filter detectors, cross-matches them with ESA Gaia DR3 optical astrometry and NASA WISE mid-infrared photometrics, and calculates least-squares proper motion vectors across survey epochs.
  • 60 FPS WebGL 3D Sky Engine: Built with Next.js and Three.js, the frontend renders a continuous 3D celestial sphere. Using custom shaders and a 4-tier Level-of-Detail (LoD) architecture, it smoothly plots over 25,000 stars without dropping frames.
  • Time-Lapse Blinking & Binary Orbit Resolver: The app includes a multi-epoch time-lapse player (Surveys 1 to 4 across 2025–2026) featuring contrast stretching, difference imaging, and Keplerian orbital decomposition for binary brown dwarfs (like Epsilon Indi Ba + Bb), allowing sub-arcsecond proper motion tracking down to 0.02′′0.02''0.02′′.
  • Real-Time Noise Calibration & Outlier Marking: Instead of blindly wiping anomalies, my algorithm samples vacant sky rings around each star to compute the local zodiacal and cosmic background radiation floor (∼0.517±0.039 MJy/sr\sim 0.517 \pm 0.039\text{ MJy/sr}∼0.517±0.039 MJy/sr), marking it with an asterisk (*). It then isolates genuine photometric spikes using a local 5-point moving median and Median Absolute Deviation (MAD×1.4826\text{MAD} \times 1.4826MAD×1.4826), tagging real anomalies with [!] so researchers can examine them.
  • Instant Deep-Link Sharing: A custom routing engine allows anyone to click "Share Link", which copies a URL with the star ID and camera coordinates (?star=...&fov=...). When opened, the camera smoothly animates and zooms into the target with 10× magnification.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero Software Barriers: Pro astronomy software like SAOImageDS9 or TOPCAT looks and feels like it was written in 1998 and requires local installations and complex scripts. Impuls runs instantly on any laptop or phone browser at 60 FPS.
  • Scientifically Honest Data: Most consumer space apps smooth out or delete noisy data to make things look pretty. Impuls keeps the raw data intact, explicitly annotating the background sky noise and flagging isolated instrument spikes so users learn how real observational astronomy works.
  • Rapid Transient & Brown Dwarf Identification: By stacking 102-band spectral SED energy curves with multi-epoch visual blinking, you can immediately tell whether a moving dot is a genuine cold brown dwarf, an eclipsing binary, or just detector scatter.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

I wanted to prove that serious scientific rigor doesn't have to be boring or inaccessible. Impuls is designed for:

  • Citizen Scientists & Students: Giving high schoolers, hobbyists, and university students the ability to inspect real NASA infrared all-sky data with publication-grade metrics without needing an astrophysicist's workstation.
  • Classroom Engagement: Teachers can share a single link (?star=Barnard's Star&fov=1.5) and immediately walk their students through proper motion, parallax, and Planck blackbody radiation curves in interactive 3D.
  • Collaborative Research: Faster visual verification of candidate objects before dedicating expensive ground or space telescope time.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python 3.10+, GLSL shader concepts, HTML5, CSS3.
  • Frontend Stack: Next.js 15 (React 19, App Router), Three.js (WebGL 3D space rendering), HTML5 <canvas> (custom 2D rendering for telemetry charts to eliminate Next.js SSR hydration mismatches), Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons.
  • Backend Stack: Flask, Astropy (WCS projection, FITS parsing), Astroquery (NASA IRSA SIA2/TAP protocol), NumPy (vectorized linear regressions and moving MAD scatter filters), Pillow.
  • Data Repositories: NASA IRSA AWS S3 Data Cubes, ESA Gaia DR3 Optical Catalog, NASA AllWISE / NEOWISE Catalog.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Multi-Wavelength Layering: Instead of looking at optical, near-IR, and thermal IR in separate tabs, Impuls synthesizes all three missions into one coherent 3D view. You can see Gaia optical stars, WISE thermal halos, and 102-band infrared spectroscopy existing simultaneously in true coordinates.
  • Observatory Functionalism: I avoided flashy, distracting sci-fi themes in favor of an austere, high-contrast, data-dense scientific design inspired by classic observatory tools. Every pixel has a purpose.
  • Canvas-Engineered Charts: Rather than relying on heavy SVG charting libraries that break during SSR hydration, I wrote custom HTML5 <canvas> renderers for the multi-band light curves, SED spectrum, and astrometric drift plots, resulting in zero-lag interaction.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Physical & Mathematical Rigor: We ensured every coordinate transformation uses real celestial geometry—especially accounting for declination compression in right ascension and keeping spectral fluxes in authentic mega-janskys per steradian.
  • The Outlier Trap: Initially, a global median threshold flagged 32 false anomalies because Planck curves naturally slope downward by an order of magnitude. I redesigned the outlier detection to use a local moving median window (±2\pm 2±2 points) and local scatter scale (4.5σ4.5\sigma4.5σ), reducing false alarms down to genuine physical spikes.
  • Hardware Agnosticism: Optimized the 3D scene using tiered geometry groups and canvas caching so that even a budget school Chromebook can render 25,000+ stars smoothly.
